title: Which clarifying questions should you ask at the start of a case?
description: The right question can split the whole case in two before you draw anything. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Ask the two or three clarifying questions whose answers would change the structure you are about to draw: usually the goal and deadline, how the client makes money, the scope, and whether the whole market is affected. If an answer would not change your plan, do not ask it. Then ask for a moment to structure your thoughts.
body:
Stage 3 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why clarifying questions matter

The right question can split the whole case in two before you draw anything. Ask whether a profit fall is industry-wide and you learn whether to look at the market or inside the company. Ask how the client makes money and you learn how to split its revenue. The firms ask for this directly: Bain's guidance tells candidates to clarify the objective before diving in, and BCG lists "clarify assumptions" among its case interview tips.

Too many questions have the opposite effect. A list of eight reads as stalling, or as someone who cannot decide what matters.

The one test for every question

Before you ask, check: would the answer change what I draw next? If yes, ask it. If no, leave it. "How many offices does the client have?" rarely passes. "Is this happening to competitors too?" almost always does in a profitability case.

This usually leaves two or three questions. That is a guide, not a rule. If the prompt already gave you the goal and the timeline, you might need only one. If the business model is unusual, you might need a third just to understand it.

Where the useful questions come from

  • The goal: "Is there a specific target, and by when?" A number and a deadline give you something to measure every later answer against.
  • The business model: "How does the client actually make money?" A commission, a subscription and advertising each split revenue differently.
  • The scope: "Are we looking at all products and countries, or just this one?"
  • The market: "Is the whole industry facing this, or just our client?"

Some case types have a natural first question. For more on each, see the framework guide by case type.

Case typeA strong first question
ProfitabilityIs the whole industry affected, or just our client?
Market entryWhat does the client already sell, and where?
AcquisitionWhy does the client want to buy: growth, capability or cost?
PricingIs this a new product, or a change to an existing price?
GrowthIs there a growth target, and over what period?

Pin down vague goals

Vague goals cause the most damage. Suppose a grocery chain wants to "improve profitability". That could mean total profit in dollars or profit margin as a percentage, and the two can point in opposite directions.

Say the chain has 10 stores, $100M of revenue and $5M of operating profit, a 5% margin. Its two weakest stores bring in $20M of revenue and $0.4M of profit, a 2% margin. Close them, and the remaining eight stores make $4.6M on $80M, a margin of 5.75%. The margin goes up, but profit falls by $0.4M. If the CEO cares about margin, closures look attractive. If the target is dollars of profit, they make things worse.

One question settles it:

"Are we trying to grow annual operating profit in dollars, or improve the operating margin?"

Then ask for time

Once your questions are answered, ask for a moment, then take it in silence:

"Thank you, that's useful. May I take a moment to structure my thoughts?"

Next comes your structure.

Weak and strong

The prompt: a mobile operator's revenue has fallen 6% in a year.

Weak: "When was the company founded? Who is the CEO? How many employees are there? What is the share price? Do they have a loyalty scheme?"
Strong: "Is the rest of the market also declining? And do we know which part is falling: contracts or pay-as-you-go?"

The strong version asks two questions, and each one decides a branch of the structure.

Common mistakes

  • Asking a long list to buy time. Ask for time openly instead.
  • Asking for facts you were already given. Check your notes first.
  • Asking for data you need later. Detailed numbers come once you have a structure. Now, ask what shapes the plan.
  • Leaving the goal vague. If there is no number, ask for one, or propose one and check it.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. A profitability case. Which single question splits the case in two?

Show a strong answer

"Is this a problem the whole industry is facing, or just our client?"

Why it works: Industry-wide points to the market. Company-only points to the client's own revenue or costs.

2. The prompt says the client "wants to grow" but gives no number. Ask about the goal.

Show a strong answer

"Is there a specific growth target, and a timeline attached to it?"

Why it works: A quantified goal is what you link every later answer back to.

3. You do not understand how the client earns money. It is a platform business.

Show a strong answer

"How does the client actually make money? Is it a commission on each transaction, a subscription or advertising?"

Why it works: The business model decides how you split revenue in your structure. See how businesses make money.

4. You have recapped and asked your questions. You need time to think.

Show a strong answer

"Thank you, that's useful. May I take a moment to structure my thoughts?"

Why it works: Silence is fine once you have asked for it.

Where to practise next

Pick five prompts from the casebook and, for each, write down only the two questions you would ask. Then compare them with the clarifications each case lists. Drill the lines with the flashcards on the perfect casing page, and see how questions fit into the first two minutes in how to open a case.
